newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - U.S. airlines to maintain 1996's success.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - U.S. airlines to maintain 1996's success.

text.p: After posting record profits in 1996, U.S. airlines will see flat earnings growth in the new year, as higher fuel costs chip away at extra revenues from the lapsed excise tax.

Major airlines will see only slim market share gains unless the long-awaited industry consolidation occurs, analysts said. "The market seems to think that this is as good as it's going to get," said Glenn Engel, an airline analyst with Goldman Sachs. "There's still some risk in airline stocks right now."

"It's unrealistic to expect to see the kinds of earnings growth rates that we saw in 1996. But if they (airlines) can maintain this, the market will respond favorably," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst at Dillon Read. "1997 still will be a very good year. We'll likely see flat year-over-year performances, but that's compared to record numbers in 1996."

Following years of volatility, some analysts see airlines entering a phase of earnings stability. International alliances, solid traffic volumes and more controlled capacity growth will help airlines post more predictable profits, analysts said.

After losing $13 billion in the first half of the decade, U.S. carriers are now flush with cash. Domestic carriers will earn about $3.6 billion in 1996, up $1.4 billion over 1995, a Merrill Lynch study said.

The eight-month lapse in the 10 percent passenger excise tax padded the airlines' coffers in 1996. Airlines enjoyed a bonus from the lapsed tax, culling funds that would have normally gone to the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration.
The carriers will enjoy another windfall this year when the excise tax expires again on Dec. 31, but analysts expect the tax to be reinstated faster -- within six months.
For each month the tax is lapsed in 1997, airlines' earnings will be about 25-26 percent higher than normal, said Brian Harris, an analyst with Lehman Brothers.

The added boost from the excise tax in 1996 helped offset a sharp rise in fuel prices. Global jet fuel prices spiked as high as $0.85 a gallon this year, up from about an average of about $0.65 a gallon last year.
Higher jet fuel prices slammed almost every U.S. carrier's earnings, except for Continental Airlines Inc, which hedged most of its fuel through early 1997.

Most analysts see fuel prices as the "great unknown" for airlines in the next year. Merrill Lynch analyst Candace Browning said she expects fuel prices to settle to about $0.65 a gallon for the full-year 1997.
The other unknown for airlines is when the much anticipated consolidation will occur, analysts said.
Most major domestic carriers have rushed to find international partners and formed loose marketing alliances. But the airlines have yet to form any major domestic marriages.

Merger speculation quieted recently after Continental said it ended merger talks with several rival carriers. Continental was said to have held preliminary talks with Delta Air Lines Inc on a deal that would have created the nation's largest airline.
Analysts differ on their views on whether the industry is ready for mega-carriers to emerge. But most agree that if one merger occurs, the other major carriers will run for partners.
USAir Group Inc, Continental, Northwest Airlines Corp and Alaska Air Group Inc remain top candidates on the acquisition list, analysts said.

Smaller carriers were hard hit in 1996 by the woes of ValuJet Inc, which was grounded in the aftermath of the Florida Everglades crash, and Kiwi International Air Lines, which suspended operations in October under a heavy debt load.
Analysts expect the smaller carriers to continue to struggle next year, while the major carriers continue to prosper.
